articles.title: New compounds target clumping enzyme to protect brain cells in Alzheimer’s models
articles.summary: An enzyme called GRK2 clumps up and damages cellular powerhouses in the brains of mice with Alzheimer's disease. Newly developed chemical compounds that prevent or eliminate these clumps helped preserve memory and slow brain cell death in the animals.

articles.title: Weight loss medications alter how the brain and kidneys manage body fluids
articles.summary: Medications like liraglutide help treat diabetes and obesity, but they also cause water loss. A new study reveals how these drugs directly lower levels of a key water-conserving hormone, altering chemical signals from the brain to the kidneys.

articles.title: Why is autism increasing? Scientists are converging on an unglamorous answer
articles.summary: Autism diagnoses have skyrocketed over the past few decades, prompting a debate among scientists. Is the biological rate of autism actually rising, or is society simply naming the condition more frequently?

articles.title: Sleep loss reduces muscle endurance by rewiring brain networks, study finds
articles.summary: Getting less than four hours of sleep severely reduces physical endurance, but not because your muscles tire out faster. A new study shows that sleep deprivation forces the brain to inefficiently rewire its neural networks, triggering premature physical exhaustion.

articles.title: Psilocybin therapy has mostly reached the well-off. A small Oregon study tested a cheaper group model for low-income patients
articles.summary: Most psychedelic research has drawn well-off participants. In a first-of-its-kind Oregon study, 19 low-income adults with depression completed group psilocybin therapy, and their average depression scores fell by more than half.

articles.title: Hiring bias against transgender women depends on both identity and appearance, field experiment suggests
articles.summary: In a field experiment involving more than 10,000 job applications in Germany, trans women who disclosed their identity or had male-coded facial features each received about 10 percent fewer positive responses from employers. When both signals were present, the penalty jumped to 32 percent.

articles.title: Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger
articles.summary: Yale scientists have uncovered how the stress hormone cortisol helps the brain turn emotional experiences into stronger, longer-lasting memories. The discovery reveals that stress can reshape communication between brain networks involved in emotion and memory, potentially explaining why certain moments are so difficult to forget.

articles.title: Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness
articles.summary: Even under general anesthesia, the human brain can analyze language, recognize different types of words, and predict what comes next in a story, according to a surprising discovery by Baylor researchers. The findings challenge our understanding of consciousness and suggest that the unconscious brain is far more capable than scientists previously realized.

Surprisingly, even white matter, once…

articles.summary: The FDA has approved the first drug that directly targets Alexander disease, a devastating neurological disorder affecting fewer than one in a million people. Developed through decades of research, Zanvastro showed promising results in clinical trials, stabilizing motor function and even improving movement in some patients.

articles.title: Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice
articles.summary: Scientists discovered that declining levels of a protein called Menin may help drive aging, and restoring it in older mice reversed several age-related changes in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing with a simple amino acid called D-serine improved memory and learning, offering a potential new approach to age-related cognitive decline.

articles.title: Eating late at night linked to up to 30% higher risk of liver disease
articles.summary: Eating late at night could be putting your liver at risk, according to a large study led by Oregon Health & Science University. Researchers analyzed data from nearly 200,000 people and found that those who regularly ate after dinner or around bedtime had a 20% to 30% higher risk of liver disease, including fatty liver disease and cirrhosis.

articles.title: Rare study reveals a striking divide inside an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain
articles.summary: A rare examination of an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain revealed that regions cleared of amyloid plaques had remarkably little of the harmful tau buildup associated with memory loss, while neighboring areas showed extensive damage. The discovery suggests that removing amyloid may have lasting protective effects and could help slow Alzheimer’s progression, especially when treatment begins early.

articles.title: A 47-year study reveals the age when your body starts losing strength
articles.summary: A 47-year study has uncovered a surprising turning point in physical aging: fitness and strength begin declining around age 35, even among people who exercise regularly. Researchers found that this decline accelerates as people get older, but starting to exercise in adulthood can still improve physical performance.

articles.title: Cancer is rising in younger adults, and scientists can't fully explain why
articles.summary: A major study found that several cancers are rising faster among younger adults in England, even as smoking, diet, and other established risk factors have generally improved. Excess weight explains only part of the increase, leaving scientists searching for other possible causes, including changes in the gut microbiome and early-life exposures.

articles.title: Scientists reveal why some workout recovery tricks can backfire
articles.summary: Ice baths, massages, compression garments, and recovery supplements promise faster muscle recovery, but research suggests their benefits are often overstated, and some techniques may even undermine long-term gains. Scientists say the most effective recovery methods are far simpler and cheaper: getting enough sleep, eating well, and giving muscles time to rebuild.
